analysis.investment_thesis: Neetu Yoshi is a freshly-listed 2020-incorporated micro-cap castings firm with barely two years of meaningful earnings and negative free cash flow every year — it fails nearly every quantitative filter I require. At a P/E of 20.4 and P/B of ~2.5 (302 Cr / 123 Cr equity), there is no margin of safety; this is a speculation on continued hyper-growth, not an investment.
key_strengths: ROE 51% and ROCE 46% indicate genuine operating earning power in 2024–25
Debt modest: borrowings 14 Cr vs equity 123 Cr (D/E ~0.11), balance sheet not stressed
Promoter holding 70% — skin in the game
key_risks: Only 2 years of meaningful profits (13 Cr, 16 Cr) — fails my 3–5 year earnings track record test
Free cash flow negative all 4 years (-1, -9, -7, -3 Cr); growth is being funded by IPO proceeds, not internal cash
P/E 20.4 and P/B ~2.5 breach Graham limits (P/E<15, P/B<1.5); no dividend history
red_flags: Recent IPO — seller (insiders/bankers) knows more than the buyer, pricing optimized for them
Equity jumped from 20 Cr to 123 Cr in 2025 (IPO infusion) — reported ROE will mechanically compress as capital is deployed
Tiny 5-year-old company in a commoditized castings/forgings industry with no demonstrated moat
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The quantitative record is simply too short. Revenue of 5 Cr in 2022 growing to 71 Cr in 2025 is impressive arithmetic, but I demand proven earning power across a full business cycle — castings and forgings are deeply cyclical, tied to steel prices, auto and railway capex, and working capital swings. Two years of profitability (2024: 13 Cr, 2025: 16 Cr) tells us nothing about how this business performs in a downturn. Worse, operating cash flow covered only 12 Cr in 2025 against 17 Cr of investing outflows, and cumulative free cash flow over four years is roughly -20 Cr. Growth has been financed by 8→14 Cr of borrowings and, decisively, a large equity raise that ballooned reserves from 16 Cr to 104 Cr.

On valuation, 302 Cr market cap against 123 Cr book is P/B ~2.5 — well above my 1.5 ceiling — and P/E 20.4 sits above my 15 threshold despite earnings that are essentially two data points. The Graham Number test fails decisively. The high ROE/ROCE are flattering in part because the denominator was tiny before the IPO; post-issue, returns on the enlarged capital base are unproven. Combined with no dividend history, an IPO premium, and a micro-cap commodity-industrial profile, this is textbook speculation. Mr. Market may be enthusiastic; I am not. Avoid.
